chunks: "I use the same loop every time. First, I define what correct looks like, from the spec or from a known-good unit.
Then I reproduce the problem and write down exactly how, because I can't debug what I can't trigger.
Next I gather evidence without changing anything: power rails, clocks, resets, currents, the simplest possible measurements, and I compare against a known-good board if I have one.
Then I narrow it down by splitting the system. If a signal chain has eight stages, I check the middle one; the problem is upstream or downstream, so I've halved the search.
I form a hypothesis, rank them by likelihood and how cheap they are to test, and test one thing at a time.
If I change two things and it gets better, I don't know which one mattered. When something fixes it, I don't stop there. I ask whether I understand why.
I verify by removing the fix and seeing the problem return, I check for side effects, and I write up the cause so the next person doesn't repeat it.

For validation it's the same mindset but proactive: start from requirements, build a test plan that covers voltage, temperature, load and unit variation, include margins and some stress cases, automate it so it's repeatable, and review the data for outliers instead of just pass or fail."
